candidate.answerReason: Substitution makes the logarithm's argument equal to \(((1+x)/(1-x))^3\). The logarithm power rule therefore gives \(G=3F\), and both functions have the same real domain.

methods.label: Factor the substituted fraction
methods.explanation:
Combining the fractions inside the logarithm reveals a useful pair of cubes. Let \(u=(3x+x^3)/(1+3x^2)\). Since \(1+3x^2>0\) for every real \(x\), this substitution introduces no zero denominator. We obtain
\[
\frac{1+u}{1-u}
=\frac{1+3x^2+3x+x^3}{1+3x^2-3x-x^3}
=\frac{(1+x)^3}{(1-x)^3}.
\]
Here the denominator is zero precisely when \(x=1\). For the logarithm to be real, its argument must be positive. Cubing preserves sign, so this condition is equivalent to \((1+x)/(1-x)>0\), or \(-1<x<1\). This is also exactly the real domain of \(F\); at \(x=-1\), the logarithm's argument is zero.

On this domain, the logarithm power rule gives
\[
G=\log\left[\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)^3\right]
=3\log\frac{1+x}{1-x}=3F.
\]
Thus the answer is \(3F\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
